messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Khalil's Story

Khalil was forty-eight when it happened—a Friday evening in late March, at a parking garage near his office in downtown Seattle. He had stayed late to finish a deployment, something he did often, something he prided himself on. The garage was nearly empty when he walked to his car. A man approached him as he unlocked the driver's side door, someone Khalil recognized vaguely from the building's security team, though they had never spoken. The man said something about needing help, asked if Khalil could come with him for a moment. Khalil, trusting and eager to be useful, agreed. What followed in the stairwell was violent and humiliating. The man had a badge, a uniform, authority that Khalil had been raised to respect. The assault lasted perhaps ten minutes but felt like an hour stretched across eternities. Khalil did not report it. He told no one. For weeks he told himself it had not happened, or that he had somehow invited it through some failure of judgment he could not quite locate.

By the time Khalil came to recognize that the assault was real and that it had fractured something in him, six months had passed. He was fifty-four now, and the fracture had only deepened. Sirens sent him into a state of acute panic—the wail of an ambulance on the street below his apartment would trigger a cascade of physical terror, his heart accelerating, his breath shortening, his mind flooding with images of the stairwell. The sound of sirens meant authority was coming, meant he was about to be found out or taken away, though he could not articulate why. Emergency vehicles, police cars, anything that suggested official response to crisis would send him into a spiral that lasted hours. Being alone with men—any men, colleagues, acquaintances, strangers in elevators—had become intolerable. His body would tense, his mind would race through scenarios of threat, and he would find excuses to leave. At work, he began declining team meetings, working from home whenever possible, telling his manager he was more productive in isolation. The truth was that the presence of men, particularly those in any position of authority, reactivated the terror of that evening with an intensity that left him shaking.

To manage the triggers, Khalil developed an architecture of avoidance that came to govern his entire existence. He stopped going anywhere near the downtown corridor where the assault had occurred, which meant abandoning his favorite coffee shop, the gym he had used for fifteen years, even the route he took to work. He rerouted his commute through neighborhoods that added forty minutes to his drive, but the detour felt necessary, a protective barrier between himself and the place where his safety had been annihilated. He avoided police and security uniforms entirely—he would cross streets to avoid officers, would leave restaurants if a uniformed guard entered, would avert his eyes from anything that suggested official authority. Military uniforms, weapons in films or on television, anything that evoked the badge and the power it represented—all of it became intolerable. He stopped watching the news. He stopped going to public spaces. His world contracted to his apartment, his car, the specific route to work, and occasionally his office building when he could time it to avoid encounters with men. The avoidance felt like survival. It felt like the only rational response to a world that had proven itself fundamentally unsafe.

What Khalil did not realize, at least not consciously, was that each act of avoidance was reinforcing the very threat system it was meant to protect him from. By refusing to go near the downtown area, by crossing streets to avoid uniforms, by isolating himself from male colleagues, he was teaching his nervous system that these things were genuinely dangerous—that his fear was justified, that the world was as threatening as his body insisted it was. The more he avoided, the more his threat detection system became hyperactive. He found himself scanning every room he entered, noting exits, tracking the position of men, monitoring the distance to safety. In the office, he would sit near the door of conference rooms, always aware of who was present, always calculating escape routes. His mind had become a surveillance system, constantly searching for signs of danger, and the searching itself became exhausting. He had come to believe that he would never feel normal again, that whatever capacity he once had for peace or ordinary human connection had been permanently destroyed. The assault had not just taken his safety; it had taken his future. And somehow, impossibly, he was certain that he had brought it on himself—that something in the way he had acted, some naive trust or weakness, had invited the violence. The injustice of it burned beneath everything: nothing had been done, no one had been held accountable, and the man still worked in the building where Khalil had once felt proud of his career.

The isolation deepened over months. Colleagues began to notice his absence from meetings, his reluctance to collaborate. His manager, concerned, had asked if everything was all right. Khalil had said nothing was wrong, just a preference for remote work, but the truth was that his job—the thing that had once given him structure and identity—was becoming impossible to maintain. He was turning down promotions, declining projects that required him to be in the office. The software he wrote was competent but uninspired; he had stopped caring about the quality of his work the way he once had. His social life had evaporated entirely. Friends had stopped calling after he declined invitations repeatedly. His family, sensing something was wrong but not knowing what, had grown distant. He spent most evenings in his apartment, the doors locked, the curtains drawn, his nervous system still braced for a threat that never came but felt perpetually imminent. It was this grinding, unrelenting exhaustion—the sense that he was disappearing, that the man he had been was already gone—that finally brought him to a therapist's office on a gray Tuesday morning. He sat in the waiting room, noting the exits, acutely aware of the male receptionist at the desk, his hands clenched in his lap. He was terrified of what talking about it would mean, terrified that speaking the truth aloud would somehow make it more real. But he was also terrified of the alternative: a life spent hiding, shrinking, waiting for a danger that had already passed but that his body could not seem to accept was over.
